management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Postpartum atony refractory to oxytocin / asthma influences uterotonics
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 33-year-old with severe asthma has persistent heavy bleeding after delivery despite uterine massage, oxytocin and appropriate resuscitation. The uterus remains soft, the placenta is complete and no major laceration is visible. The obstetric team is considering a second-line uterotonic and mechanical measures; a junior suggests carboprost without reviewing the respiratory history.
ask: Which management principle is most important in choosing further treatment?
options: Repeat oxytocin indefinitely without considering other treatments or mechanical haemostasis.
Give carboprost routinely because it cannot affect bronchial smooth muscle function.
Stop resuscitation temporarily while waiting for the uterus to contract spontaneously.
Choose any uterotonic solely by cost because respiratory comorbidity is irrelevant.
Avoid carboprost in severe asthma and escalate to suitable alternatives or mechanical control.
explanations: Ongoing severe bleeding requires escalating pharmacological and mechanical treatment, not indefinite repetition of one agent.
Carboprost can precipitate bronchospasm; asthma is an important precaution or contraindication depending on severity and local guidance.
Resuscitation must continue alongside uterine management, as hypovolaemia may become life-threatening.
The safety profile matters: uterotonics have distinct cardiovascular and respiratory contraindications.
Correct. In severe asthma, carboprost is generally avoided because of bronchospasm risk; consider alternatives such as misoprostol and balloon tamponade under the PPH protocol.
pearl: The next uterotonic in PPH depends on comorbidities: carboprost can cause bronchospasm, while ergometrine is problematic in hypertension.
pivot: With hypertension or pre-eclampsia, ergometrine is also unsuitable; consider drug-specific contraindications and mechanical escalation.

steps: Identify persistent atonic PPH despite first-line measures and assess shock.
Review asthma severity, blood pressure, contraindications and bleeding volume.
Continue blood-product support and use safe second-line uterotonics or balloon measures.
Escalate rapidly to theatre and definitive surgical haemostasis if bleeding continues.
management.safety: Do not administer carboprost reflexively to a patient with severe asthma.
management.local: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Primary postpartum haemorrhage.

skill: Acute coronary syndrome / early antiplatelet
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 62-year-old with hypertension reports 45 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. ECG shows new anterior ST depression; she is alert with BP 138/82 mmHg and no active bleeding. She has never had an aspirin allergy and has not received any medications for this episode.
ask: Which treatment should be administered promptly while definitive ACS assessment proceeds?
options: Give a chewable loading dose of aspirin unless contraindicated, alongside the ACS pathway.
Delay all antiplatelet therapy until the second troponin has confirmed myocardial necrosis.
Give thrombolysis immediately because any ischaemic ST-segment change indicates STEMI.
Give high-dose intravenous heparin alone without aspirin or diagnostic reassessment.
Start a prophylactic oral antibiotic because myocardial injury may reflect an infection.
explanations: Correct. Early aspirin reduces platelet aggregation and is standard initial treatment for suspected ACS when there is no contraindication; continue ECG/troponin and risk assessment.
A high clinical suspicion of ACS warrants aspirin before repeat troponin confirmation, barring bleeding or allergy.
ST depression suggests ischaemia but is not a standard STEMI fibrinolysis indication; evaluate the full ECG and clinical context.
Anticoagulation may be indicated after assessment, but it does not replace aspirin and should follow an appropriate pathway.
Antibiotics do not treat plaque rupture or coronary thrombosis; there is no evidence of infection.
pearl: Early chewable aspirin is appropriate for suspected ACS unless allergy or major bleeding risk prohibits it.
pivot: If aortic dissection is strongly suspected, reassess before antithrombotics because bleeding consequences may be catastrophic.

steps: Assess ABCs, obtain 12-lead ECG promptly and review haemodynamics.
Give aspirin loading dose when not contraindicated and obtain serial troponin.
Apply risk-based ACS therapy and seek cardiology input for invasive evaluation.
Monitor pain, rhythm and bleeding while updating the diagnosis.
management.safety: Do not give nitrates to hypotensive patients or those with relevant phosphodiesterase inhibitor exposure.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Aortic dissection / avoid premature anticoagulation
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 60-year-old develops sudden maximal-intensity chest pain tearing through to the back while lifting a heavy box. He has a new pulse deficit in the left arm and systolic BP differs by 35 mmHg between arms. ECG shows no ST elevation, and a colleague proposes treating presumed ACS with full-dose anticoagulation.
ask: What is the best immediate diagnostic strategy in this stable patient?
options: Administer therapeutic heparin first and request CT only if serial troponins become positive.
Arrange urgent CT angiography of the aorta with vascular or cardiothoracic escalation.
Use a D-dimer alone to exclude dissection because the ECG lacks diagnostic changes.
Perform exercise stress testing to reproduce the chest pain before specialist referral.
Discharge after analgesia if the first troponin and portable chest X-ray are normal.
explanations: Heparin may worsen bleeding in dissection and should not be started blindly when classic dissection red flags are present.
Correct. Abrupt tearing pain with pulse/BP asymmetry raises acute aortic syndrome; urgent CTA defines anatomy in a stable patient and prompts surgical planning.
D-dimer can contribute only in selected low-probability pathways and cannot replace imaging in a high-suspicion case.
Stress testing is unsafe in possible acute aortic pathology and is not a diagnostic test for dissection.
Normal early troponin or chest radiograph cannot exclude aortic dissection and do not justify discharge.
pearl: Pulse deficit plus abrupt tearing pain is aortic dissection until urgently excluded; antithrombotics may be harmful.
pivot: Unstable patients may need immediate bedside echocardiography and operative consultation rather than transport to CT.

steps: Assess haemodynamics, limb pulses and neurological signs.
Obtain urgent CTA when stable and seek immediate specialist advice.
Provide controlled analgesia and specialist-directed heart-rate/BP management.
Monitor for tamponade, malperfusion and need for emergency surgery.
management.safety: Do not allow a normal ECG or chest X-ray to reassure you against a high-risk dissection.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Child head injury / deterioration during observation
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A seven-year-old falls from a scooter and initially has GCS 15 without focal deficits. After two hours of emergency-department observation he becomes progressively sleepy, repeatedly vomits and now has GCS 13. His pupils are equal, but he is slower to follow commands than at triage.
ask: What is the safest immediate management?
options: Continue the existing observation schedule because equal pupils exclude intracranial bleeding.
Provide an antiemetic and discharge if vomiting settles before the next assessment.
Arrange urgent senior review and neuroimaging with resuscitation readiness.
Reassure the parents that drowsiness is a normal consequence of mild concussion.
Defer reassessment until the next day because the initial GCS was fully normal.
explanations: A fall in GCS is a high-risk sign even with equal pupils; routine observation without escalation is unsafe.
Symptom treatment cannot substitute for investigating deterioration in conscious state.
Correct. GCS decline of two points with repeated vomiting demands immediate senior review, consideration of CT and preparedness for neurological resuscitation.
Concussion is possible but cannot be assumed when consciousness worsens after a head injury.
An initially normal examination does not rule out evolving intracranial injury; delays risk irreversible deterioration.
pearl: A drop of at least two GCS points during observation is an emergency red flag after paediatric head injury.
pivot: A well child with isolated vomiting and otherwise normal examination may be observed rather than immediately scanned.

steps: Repeat ABCDE and document serial GCS, pupils and limb power.
Call senior emergency/neurosurgical help and arrange urgent CT as indicated.
Support airway and circulation and treat raised intracranial pressure if suspected.
Reassess frequently and communicate deterioration to caregivers.
management.safety: Do not discharge a child whose consciousness or neurological examination has worsened.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Lactational breast abscess / imaging and drainage
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A breastfeeding woman at six weeks postpartum returns after four days of worsening unilateral breast pain and fever despite prescribed flucloxacillin. She has a localised tender fluctuant mass near the areola and persistent temperature 38.6°C. Her infant continues to feed well, and she asks whether antibiotics alone are enough to cure the new lump.
ask: What additional management is now most appropriate?
options: Stop breastfeeding permanently and prescribe oral cabergoline before investigating the breast mass.
Increase pumping frequency every hour and apply vigorous deep massage to disperse the lump.
Change to a different oral antibiotic without examining the fluctuant collection further.
Arrange breast ultrasound and drainage of a suspected abscess while continuing appropriate therapy.
Provide reassurance because focal fluctuance is expected during uncomplicated inflammatory mastitis.
explanations: Lactation suppression is not routinely necessary and can worsen engorgement; management should focus on diagnosing and draining a collection.
Over-pumping and aggressive massage may worsen tissue inflammation and cannot reliably empty an abscess cavity.
Changing antibiotics without source control may fail when a pus collection has developed.

Correct. Persistent fever with focal fluctuance despite antibiotics suggests breast abscess; ultrasound and aspiration or drainage are indicated, with compatible antibiotics and breastfeeding support.
A fluctuant mass with persistent systemic symptoms is not ordinary inflammatory mastitis and warrants prompt imaging.
pearl: Focal fluctuance and persistent fever despite treatment suggest an abscess requiring drainage, not simply stronger antibiotics.
pivot: Early mastitis without fluctuance or prolonged fever often responds to anti-inflammatory care and cue-based feeding.

steps: Identify persistent fever and focal fluctuance after antibiotic treatment.
Arrange breast ultrasound and assess for sepsis and feeding difficulties.
Obtain aspiration or drainage with culture and appropriate antibiotic cover.
Support continued breastfeeding when feasible and confirm clinical resolution.
management.safety: Do not repeatedly prescribe antibiotics without evaluating a possible drainable collection.
management.local: Queensland maternity and lactation guidance.

skill: Post-attempt discharge planning / rapid aftercare and warm handover
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 35-year-old is medically stable following treatment for a self-poisoning episode. A senior mental health clinician has completed a comprehensive assessment, and a collaborative discharge plan with family supervision and means restriction is considered safe. The patient has no current suicidal intent, but has missed several previous outpatient appointments. The ward asks how to reduce risk during the transition home.
ask: Which discharge arrangement best strengthens continuity of care?
options: Provide a generic brochure and advise the patient to book their own appointment in a month.
Send the discharge summary without confirming that any service has accepted the referral.
Rely on the family alone because the absence of current intent eliminates post-discharge risk.
Wait until the patient requests counselling again before arranging mental health contact.
Arrange rapid suicide aftercare contact with a warm handover and documented safety plan.
explanations: Generic information and delayed self-booking leave a high-risk post-crisis gap, especially after prior missed appointments.
Sending paperwork alone does not establish engagement; a named receiving team and contact plan improve continuity.
Family support helps but cannot replace coordinated follow-up after a recent attempt.
A passive approach is risky because the period after discharge remains vulnerable even without current intent.
Correct. Rapid aftercare, ideally contact within one or two business days, plus an agreed safety plan and warm handover can reduce loss to follow-up.
pearl: The post-attempt transition is a vulnerable period; warm handover and rapid aftercare are active safety interventions.
pivot: If imminent intent or inability to remain safe returns, discharge planning should stop and emergency reassessment is required.

steps: Confirm completed acute assessment and a clinically safe disposition.
Review supports, access to means, prior disengagement and transport barriers.
Arrange warm handover to rapid aftercare and document a collaborative safety plan.
Confirm early contact, crisis pathways and escalation if follow-up fails.
management.safety: Aftercare cannot substitute for inpatient safety when acute risk remains high.
management.local: NSW ACI Universal Aftercare guidance.

skill: Coronial reporting / traumatic cause of death
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: An 82-year-old man is admitted to a Victorian hospital after slipping on wet steps and fracturing his hip. Despite treatment, he develops complications of immobility and dies three weeks later. His treating team knows his medical history and the death was expected during his last hospital day. A junior doctor is asked to complete the routine medical certificate of cause of death without contacting anyone else.
ask: What is the most appropriate response by the treating doctor?
options: Notify the coroner because the death followed an accidental injury, even after a delay.
Complete the ordinary certificate because the terminal illness was predictable during admission.
Complete the certificate because verification of death was performed by a senior doctor.
Treat the death as entirely natural because there was no immediate operative complication.
Await written family consent before deciding whether a coroner report is legally needed.
explanations: Correct. In Victoria, a death arising directly or indirectly from an accident or injury is reportable, even if the person dies much later from complications. Verify the death and follow the coroner notification process.
A predictable terminal course does not override the requirement to report a death connected to accidental injury. Do not assume that predictable means natural.
Verification confirms that death occurred; certification addresses its probable medical cause. Neither verification by a senior nor familiarity with the patient removes coronial duties.
The original traumatic injury remains relevant in the causal chain. A natural-looking terminal event does not by itself convert an injury-related death into a non-reportable one.
The family should receive respectful communication, but their consent is not a prerequisite for meeting a legal reporting obligation. Escalate uncertainty to the coronial service.
pearl: Verification of death, medical certification and coronial reporting are different tasks; an injury-related death may require reporting weeks later.
pivot: An expected death due solely to advanced naturally occurring disease may be certifiable by the treating team if the cause is known and no reporting criteria apply.

steps: Verify and document the death, circumstances and causal sequence.
Review clinical records and discuss the accidental fall with a senior clinician.
Notify Victoria's coronial service rather than issuing a routine certificate.
Communicate with family and comply with coronial documentation and local policy.
management.safety: Australian coronial rules differ by jurisdiction; this stem is specifically Victorian.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Stoma ischaemia / urgent senior surgical escalation
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: Four days after formation of an end colostomy, a 73-year-old reports mild worsening abdominal discomfort. The ward nurse says the stoma looks increasingly dark purple and almost black at its tip. The surface is dry and does not bleed when gently touched; output has fallen. He is mildly tachycardic but has no frank hypotension. The appliance has leaked once overnight.
ask: Which action should take priority?
options: Request routine stoma-therapy review for a new appliance and skin-barrier fitting.
Escalate immediately to the surgical registrar for possible stoma ischaemia.
Administer a large laxative dose to increase output through the new colostomy.
Order routine abdominal radiography before notifying the responsible surgical team.
Observe the colour until the next morning because darkening is usual in new stomas.
explanations: Stoma nursing is useful for skin and appliance care, but a dry dark stoma with absent bleeding raises concern for compromised blood supply, not just leakage.

Correct. Dusky, black or non-bleeding mucosa suggests stoma ischaemia/necrosis. Prompt senior surgical assessment determines depth and the need for urgent intervention; resuscitation and investigations proceed as indicated.
A laxative does not restore blood flow and may worsen discomfort or risk in a patient with possible postoperative complications.
Imaging may help clarify deeper complications, but should not be a prerequisite for calling the surgeon about possible ischaemic tissue.
Normal stomas are typically viable and moist red/pink. Progressive darkening without contact bleeding is not a routine expected postoperative change.
pearl: Colour, moisture, bleeding and output tell you more about stoma viability than the condition of the bag.
pivot: Peristomal skin irritation with a pink, moist functioning stoma can be managed with routine stoma nursing advice.

steps: Assess vitals, abdominal findings, stoma colour and output.
Check perfusion, blood tests and whether there are signs of systemic compromise.
Call the treating surgical registrar immediately and keep the patient fasting if theatre is possible.
Monitor for worsening pain, peritonitis and deterioration while the surgical plan is made.
management.safety: Do not allow an appliance problem to distract from stoma necrosis; delay may cost viable bowel.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: TRALI / noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema after blood products
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 38-year-old receives packed red cells during major abdominal surgery. Two hours into recovery he becomes breathless, febrile and hypoxaemic. Chest radiography shows new bilateral airspace opacities. Blood pressure is 92/56 mmHg, JVP is not elevated, and fluid balance is only mildly positive. Bedside echocardiography does not indicate raised left-sided filling pressures.
ask: Which process best explains the acute deterioration?
options: A transfusion-associated circulatory overload syndrome causing hydrostatic pulmonary oedema.
A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction producing isolated renal damage days later.
Transfusion-related acute lung injury producing bilateral noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
Unilateral re-expansion pulmonary oedema following evacuation of a large pneumothorax.
Fat embolism related to fracture of a major long bone during a separate injury.
explanations: TACO more often presents with hypertension, positive fluid balance, raised JVP or other signs of circulatory overload; these are not supported here.
Delayed haemolytic reactions typically occur later and have features such as falling haemoglobin or jaundice; they do not neatly explain new acute bilateral infiltrates within two hours.

Correct. TRALI can cause acute hypoxaemia and bilateral infiltrates during or within six hours of transfusion, without left-sided volume overload. Stop the transfusion and give respiratory and haemodynamic support.
Re-expansion oedema generally follows re-expansion of the affected lung, which is not described, and often has a unilateral pattern.
Fat embolism generally follows long-bone or pelvic trauma and commonly develops later with neurological signs or petechiae; none is described.
pearl: TRALI is acute noncardiogenic respiratory deterioration within six hours of transfusion; compare with TACO before prescribing diuretics.
pivot: If raised JVP, fluid overload and hypertension dominate after transfusion, TACO is more likely and fluid reduction/diuresis can help.

steps: Stop any ongoing transfusion and activate a transfusion reaction response.
Provide oxygen and critical-care assessment, then evaluate imaging and cardiac filling pressures.
Support breathing and circulation; discuss findings with haematology and the transfusion service.
Document reaction and coordinate Lifeblood notification and component investigation.
management.safety: Diuretics are not beneficial for TRALI and can worsen hypotension; avoid assuming all post-transfusion pulmonary oedema is TACO.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis / limited renal compensation
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 76-year-old with chronic lung disease arrives with marked increased work of breathing. An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.21, PaCO₂ 64 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 26 mmol/L and PaO₂ 53 mmHg on room air. The admitting doctor notes that bicarbonate is near normal despite severe acidaemia. The patient was alert earlier but is becoming fatigued.
ask: What is the most accurate interpretation of this gas?
options: Primary metabolic acidosis with inadequate respiratory compensation and concomitant normal oxygenation.
Chronic compensated respiratory acidosis with a near-normal hydrogen ion concentration.
Predominant respiratory alkalosis causing reduced bicarbonate from chronic renal compensation.
Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis with associated hypoxaemia and little metabolic compensation.
Mixed metabolic alkalosis and hyperventilation explaining low oxygenation in this patient.
explanations: A primary metabolic acidosis would generally involve a reduced bicarbonate; here marked carbon dioxide elevation explains the low pH, and oxygenation is also poor.
Chronic renal compensation would tend to raise bicarbonate more, and the low pH argues against a well-compensated chronic state.
Respiratory alkalosis requires reduced rather than raised PaCO₂, and renal bicarbonate reduction does not match these data.

Correct. CO₂ is high and pH is low, while bicarbonate has risen little, indicating acute respiratory acidaemia with hypoxaemia. Escalate support according to clinical status and local ventilatory criteria.
There is no evidence of a raised bicarbonate indicating metabolic alkalosis, nor of low CO₂ from hyperventilation.
pearl: Acute respiratory acidosis: low pH, high PaCO₂ and only modest bicarbonate change; rising CO₂ with fatigue signals danger.
pivot: A chronic CO₂ retainer may have a higher baseline bicarbonate and a less depressed pH even at similar PaCO₂.

steps: Rapidly assess consciousness, ventilation, oxygenation and airway protection.
Review blood gas, baseline gases, imaging and reversible respiratory triggers.
Provide controlled oxygen and consider ventilatory support through the appropriate team.
Repeat gases and escalate for worsening fatigue, acidaemia or hypercapnia.
management.safety: Do not assume normal oxygen saturation on supplemental oxygen excludes carbon dioxide narcosis or ventilatory failure.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Burn involving the hand / specialist referral for function
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 42-year-old spills boiling tea across the back of his dominant hand. He receives appropriate first aid, and the injured area is very painful, pink, moist and blanches with light pressure. Several small blisters are present; the affected area covers much less than 1% of total body surface area. He has full finger movement at present.
ask: Which feature most strengthens the need for early specialist assessment?
options: The presence of severe pain despite reassuring capillary refill and pink appearance.
The blistered appearance despite preserved movement and minimal body surface area.
The brief blanching after pressure that indicates dermal perfusion remains present.
The small proportion of total body surface area involved in the injury.
The involvement of a functionally important hand with risk of scarring and contracture.
explanations: Pain helps assess and treat the injury but does not independently determine the referral threshold.
Blisters suggest partial-thickness injury, but size and depth must be interpreted with function and anatomical site.
Blanching may indicate a more superficial dermal component; it does not outweigh anatomical function considerations.
A small total area often means fluid resuscitation is unnecessary, but does not remove risk of hand contracture or functional impairment.

Correct. Even small burns of hands warrant early specialist discussion because healing, movement and scarring can impair grip and fine motor function. Cooling, analgesia, dressings and hand therapy remain relevant.
pearl: Burn referral depends on the site and function as well as area and depth.
pivot: Extensive burns or suspected inhalation injury require a separate major-burn resuscitation pathway.

steps: Provide appropriate cool running water first aid, analgesia and initial assessment.
Assess depth, circulation, finger movement and tetanus status.
Apply suitable dressings and seek early burns/hand specialist advice.
Plan functional rehabilitation, dressings and scar prevention.
management.safety: Do not dismiss a hand burn simply because it occupies a tiny percentage of body surface area.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Painless late-pregnancy bleeding / placenta previa precautions
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 30-year-old at 35 weeks' gestation arrives after sudden bright-red vaginal bleeding while resting. She has no uterine tenderness, contractions or trauma. Her booking ultrasound report is unavailable. Heart rate is 115/min and blood pressure is 105/67 mmHg. A student proposes an immediate digital vaginal examination to check cervical dilation.
ask: What is the safest next management direction?
options: Resuscitate and assess fetal wellbeing while avoiding digital vaginal examination until placental site is known.
Perform a digital vaginal examination first because painless bleeding usually arises from the cervix.
Prescribe tocolysis and send her home as absence of contractions excludes obstetric bleeding risk.
Begin labour induction immediately without ultrasound or specialist obstetric assessment.
Reassure and observe at home because significant bleeding from placental abruption is always painful.
explanations: Correct. Painless late pregnancy bleeding suggests possible placenta previa. Assess maternal stability, fetal status, blood loss and placental localisation with urgent obstetric involvement; avoid digital examination until previa is excluded.
A finger examination could trigger catastrophic haemorrhage if placenta covers the cervical os and should not precede placental localisation.
Absence of contractions does not make third-trimester bleeding benign. Tocolysis and discharge are unsafe before diagnosing the source.
Delivery planning depends on haemodynamics, gestation, placental position and fetal condition; immediate unsupervised induction could be dangerous.
Abruption is often painful but not universally so. The bleeding requires urgent maternity assessment regardless of differential diagnosis.
pearl: Painless antepartum haemorrhage suggests placenta previa; do not perform digital vaginal examination until placental location is established.
pivot: Painful bleeding with a tender or rigid uterus raises concern for abruption, but either presentation demands urgent assessment.

steps: Initiate obstetric emergency assessment and appropriate monitoring.
Establish maternal IV access, blood tests and fetal wellbeing assessment.
Request urgent ultrasound placental localisation and senior management.
Arrange observation, haemorrhage readiness and delivery planning based on findings.
management.safety: Placenta previa must be excluded before a digital vaginal examination in late pregnancy bleeding.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Fever and delirium with catheter / source evaluation
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: An 86-year-old usually living independently becomes abruptly confused and drowsy at his nursing facility. He has a long-term urinary catheter and a temperature of 38.7°C. BP is 125/76 mmHg, lungs are clear and abdominal examination is non-tender. A bag specimen collected from the catheter two weeks ago grew mixed bacteria, and staff assume it confirms the current source.
ask: Which approach best tests the suspected cause while avoiding a misleading result?
options: Start treatment based solely on the older bag culture because long-term catheters remain sterile.
Use a newly collected catheter-system specimen for culture while assessing other causes of febrile delirium.
Send a swab of the old urine drainage bag because it preserves bacterial growth over time.
Order immediate CT brain as the only investigation because urinary infection cannot cause delirium.
Assume bacteriuria proves symptomatic infection and omit blood tests and clinical reassessment.
explanations: A two-week-old bag result is not a reliable current culture and cannot prove symptomatic infection. Long-term catheters commonly develop colonisation.

Correct. Fever and delirium warrant prompt sepsis/delirium assessment, cultures and source investigation; replace the long-standing catheter when indicated and obtain a fresh urine sample from the appropriate sampling port or new system.
The drainage bag is commonly contaminated and should not be used as the source of a diagnostic urine culture.
Neuroimaging is considered when there are focal signs, trauma or another neurological indication; it is not automatically the most useful first test here.
Bacteriuria is frequent with long-term catheters. The clinical context matters, and simultaneous examination for alternative infection or metabolic triggers is required.
pearl: Long-term urinary catheters often harbour bacteria; symptoms and a properly collected culture are essential to interpret the result.
pivot: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheter users generally should not be treated except for specific clinical indications.

steps: Assess delirium, sepsis physiology, glucose, medications and hydration.
Review catheter age and obtain a fresh appropriate urine specimen and other cultures as indicated.
Treat clinically suspected infection using local antibiotic protocol while assessing other sources.
Review cultures, replace catheter when appropriate and plan delirium recovery care.
management.safety: Do not culture an old drainage bag or equate a positive result with symptomatic catheter infection.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: New photopsia/floaters / retinal tear risk
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 61-year-old notices dozens of new black spots drifting across the vision of one eye, followed by brief flashes of light in the temporal field. There is no headache, eye pain or drug use. She can still read normal-sized print, but describes a small dark shadow beginning at the far peripheral field. The GP can offer review in two weeks or contact an acute eye service today.
ask: What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Treat as visual hallucinations related to stress and arrange routine psychological review.
Recommend lubricating drops and observe because visual acuity remains largely preserved.
Arrange urgent dilated retinal examination for a possible retinal tear or detachment.
Request a routine visual field appointment before considering any retinal examination.
Begin empirical systemic corticosteroids because photopsia indicates optic neuritis.
explanations: New floaters and flashes, especially with a shadow, have an ocular pattern that is not characteristic of primary psychiatric visual hallucinations.
Artificial tears may relieve surface irritation but do not address a potentially detached or torn retina.
Correct. New flashes, floaters and a curtain or shadow warrant urgent ophthalmic assessment to detect a retinal tear or developing detachment before sight is lost.
Formal field testing may document deficit but must not delay dilated fundus examination when retinal detachment is possible.
Optic neuritis usually presents with reduced central vision and pain on eye movement; these symptoms more strongly suggest vitreoretinal traction.
pearl: Flashes, new floaters and a curtain-like shadow are retinal-detachment warning signs, even if central vision remains good.
pivot: Longstanding unchanged floaters without flashes, shadow or reduction in vision may be less urgent but still deserve appropriate history.

steps: Record onset, laterality, field shadow, trauma and visual acuity.
Contact urgent ophthalmic assessment for dilated retinal examination.
Avoid delaying specialist referral for routine optometry waiting lists.
Advise immediate return with worsening shadow or visual loss and document plan.
management.safety: Retinal detachment can progress despite preserved reading vision; do not defer evaluation because acuity is normal.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Primary aldosteronism / hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 47-year-old has repeated blood pressure readings around 184/102 mmHg despite no regular medication. She reports increasing muscle weakness and cramps. Potassium is 2.7 mmol/L, sodium 141 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L and creatinine is normal. She has no vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretic use or episodes of palpitations with headache and sweating.
ask: Which investigation most directly evaluates the likely secondary cause of hypertension?
options: A single resting plasma metanephrine concentration without any endocrine preparation.
A random urinary cortisol measurement to diagnose glucocorticoid excess immediately.
A thyroid-stimulating hormone assay as the sole test for renal potassium wasting.
An aldosterone-to-renin ratio with correction of potassium and medication review.
A 24-hour urine catecholamine screen as the only initial diagnostic investigation.
explanations: Phaeochromocytoma can cause episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, but the sustained hypertension plus low potassium is more characteristic of aldosterone excess.
A random urinary cortisol cannot diagnose Cushing syndrome, and the hallmark pattern here is mineralocorticoid-related sodium retention with potassium loss.
Thyroid dysfunction may affect blood pressure, but does not typically cause this severe unexplained hypokalaemia and sustained hypertension.
Correct. Screen for primary aldosteronism with aldosterone-renin testing, after correcting hypokalaemia where possible and accounting for medicines that distort the ratio.
Catecholamine testing can evaluate suspected phaeochromocytoma but is not most targeted when spontaneous hypokalaemia accompanies sustained severe hypertension.
pearl: Severe or resistant hypertension with unexplained hypokalaemia should prompt primary aldosteronism screening.
pivot: Hypokalaemia can suppress aldosterone and mislead testing; sample conditions and medication interference matter.

steps: Assess severe hypertension and symptoms of end-organ injury.
Correct low potassium and review medicines affecting renin or aldosterone.
Order aldosterone-renin ratio and specialist confirmatory pathway.
Manage blood pressure and arrange subtype classification if confirmed.
management.safety: Do not rush to CT of adrenal glands without biochemical work-up and specialist interpretation.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Epistaxis after warfarin / tests after bleeding stops
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 78-year-old with atrial fibrillation and previous stroke takes warfarin. She comes to the ED after prolonged unilateral epistaxis; a nurse has applied 15 minutes of correct pressure and topical vasoconstrictor, and bleeding has now ceased. BP is 99/62 mmHg, HR 112/min, she looks pale, and nobody knows her latest INR. She is not currently choking or bleeding briskly.
ask: What should be prioritised next?
options: Discharge immediately because successful direct pressure means further assessment is unnecessary.
Reverse warfarin with IV vitamin K before checking whether anticoagulation is excessive.
Insert bilateral nasal packs despite cessation of bleeding to prevent any possible recurrence.
Begin a routine observation period without assessing blood loss or anticoagulation status.
Obtain haemoglobin, coagulation/INR and appropriate blood bank testing while reassessing perfusion.
explanations: Successful local control does not exclude important blood loss or excessive anticoagulation; pallor, tachycardia and low BP demand evaluation.
Reversal may be required for major ongoing bleeding or a dangerous coagulopathy, but not every controlled nosebleed warrants automatic reversal without assessing INR, severity and thrombotic risk.
Packing is generally for bleeding that continues or recurs despite first aid and targeted treatments; unnecessary packing can cause harm.
Observation may ultimately be needed, but deciding its location and safety requires assessment of blood loss and anticoagulation.
Correct. Reassess haemodynamics, check haemoglobin and INR/coagulation and consider group-and-hold or crossmatch depending on severity, then decide on reversal and observation with senior input.
pearl: After epistaxis stops, assess volume loss and anticoagulation before discharge or automatic reversal.
pivot: Active life-threatening epistaxis requires haemorrhage control, resuscitation and urgent ENT support before waiting for test results.

steps: Reassess airway, bleeding, BP, pulse and clinical perfusion.
Check FBC, INR/coagulation and blood bank sample when indicated.
Plan observation, anticoagulant management or ENT treatment based on severity.
Document return advice and review of thrombotic and bleeding risks.
management.safety: Warfarin reversal decisions weigh haemorrhage severity and stroke risk; never reverse reflexively without clinical assessment.
management.local: Current Australian practice; assess with senior clinicians and local pathways.

skill: Uncomplicated lumbar radiculopathy / conservative initial care
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 36-year-old develops severe low back pain radiating into his right calf after lifting furniture yesterday. Tingling is confined to the dorsum of his right foot. He has a positive straight-leg raise but normal ankle dorsiflexion strength, reflexes and walking balance. He reports no saddle sensory change, bladder problems, fever or cancer history. Analgesia improves his ability to mobilise.
ask: Beyond initial analgesia and advice, what is the best next plan?
options: Encourage graded activity and physiotherapy with review if symptoms persist or red flags develop.
Obtain an urgent lumbar MRI because any isolated sensory symptom proves dangerous compression.
Refer for emergency spinal decompression despite preserved motor function and continence.
Request inflammatory blood tests and vertebral imaging before allowing any mobilisation.
Arrange immediate nerve-root injection because severe pain proves conservative care will fail.
explanations: Correct. Acute radicular pain with no progressive weakness or cauda equina features usually starts with education, tolerable activity, physiotherapy and reassessment; routine emergency imaging is not indicated.
Sensory radiculopathy is common and alone does not mandate urgent MRI. Image urgently with saddle symptoms, bladder or bowel dysfunction, progressive weakness or other concerning features.
Emergency surgery targets serious compression or progressing deficits, neither established by this examination. Referral may be appropriate if symptoms fail to improve.
No constitutional or infection signs suggest a need for routine inflammatory markers. Unnecessary bed rest and delaying movement can impair recovery.
Epidural injection is sometimes considered for persistent disabling symptoms after clinical review; it is not automatically the first intervention on day one.
pearl: Severe pain alone does not mandate urgent MRI when neurologic power, reflexes and sphincter function are preserved.
pivot: New retention, saddle anaesthesia, progressive weakness or bilateral neurological change requires urgent MRI/spinal assessment.

steps: Check motor power, sensation, reflexes and all serious spinal red flags.
Avoid routine early imaging if findings remain reassuring.
Provide multimodal analgesia, activity advice and physiotherapy.
Safety-net for new deficits and reassess persistent or worsening pain.
management.safety: Do not confuse high pain severity with cauda equina syndrome; ask urinary and saddle-sensation questions explicitly.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Cellulitis versus DVT / discriminatory ipsilateral lymphadenopathy
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 51-year-old with diabetes reports two days of worsening tenderness and redness over one calf. There is a warm irregular 8-cm erythematous patch after a small scratch, a small amount of unilateral swelling and a temperature of 37.8°C. He has palpable varicose veins but no recent operation, immobilisation or known thrombophilia. Several tender enlarged nodes are felt in the groin on the same side.
ask: Which finding most directly favours a local skin infection over venous thrombosis?
options: The slight rise in temperature without a recorded temperature above 38°C.
The tender regional lymph nodes draining the inflamed skin on the same leg.
The visible superficial varicose veins present before the painful episode started.
The minor difference in calf circumference measured at the bedside.
The absence of dyspnoea and chest pain despite unilateral calf swelling.
explanations: Mild temperature elevation may accompany either inflammation or infection and is not highly discriminating on its own.
Correct. Regional tender lymphadenopathy reflects a local inflammatory or infectious drainage response, supporting cellulitis. It does not definitively exclude DVT if thromboembolic risk remains.
Varicose veins can contribute to venous symptoms or superficial thrombophlebitis, but are common and do not identify the current cause.
Mild calf swelling is nonspecific and can occur in cellulitis, DVT or venous disease. Consider objective DVT assessment if probability remains significant.
DVT can exist without pulmonary symptoms. Their absence cannot exclude venous thrombosis and does not identify the origin of a red skin patch.
pearl: Tender draining lymph nodes favour cellulitis; assess DVT probability separately when it remains clinically plausible.
pivot: Diffuse swelling with little skin inflammation and substantial thrombotic risk may prompt compression ultrasonography.

steps: Examine skin breaks, spreading erythema, nodes and distal perfusion.
Assess fever, systemic illness and clinical pretest probability of DVT.
Use indicated cellulitis antibiotics and supportive measures or DVT testing if warranted.
Mark skin margins and arrange review if redness spreads or systemic symptoms develop.
management.safety: Never use lymphadenopathy as a stand-alone test to rule out DVT; serious skin infection signs also demand escalation.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Intermittent palpitations / ambulatory ECG selection
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 32-year-old teacher describes sudden episodes of very rapid regular heartbeat lasting three to eight minutes. They have occurred every afternoon for the past five days and terminate abruptly, occasionally while resting. There has been no syncope, chest pain or exertional trigger. Examination, FBC, thyroid function and a resting 12-lead ECG are normal when she is asymptomatic.
ask: Which test is most likely to establish the rhythm responsible?
options: Serial troponin measurements while the patient remains pain free in the GP waiting room.
Repeated spot ECGs at arbitrary times when she reports no ongoing palpitations.
A 24–48-hour ambulatory ECG monitor given the near-daily frequency of events.
A plain chest radiograph to detect the electrical origin of the palpitation episodes.
A formal sleep study before recording any symptom-associated electrocardiographic signal.
explanations: Troponin assesses possible myocardial injury and does not usually determine the nature of recurrent brief arrhythmias without ischaemic symptoms.
An ECG between spells may remain entirely normal despite SVT or intermittent atrial arrhythmia; repeated unscheduled recordings can miss events.
Correct. Frequent near-daily symptoms are suitable for Holter or ambulatory ECG monitoring to correlate symptoms with rhythm; less frequent events need a longer recorder.
Chest imaging may be useful for structural or pulmonary indications but will not capture transient electrical arrhythmia episodes.
Sleep investigations are not the primary test for abrupt daytime palpitations with a normal examination and absent sleep symptoms.
pearl: A normal resting ECG does not exclude SVT; select ambulatory-monitor duration based on how often symptoms occur.
pivot: Infrequent monthly episodes are better suited to longer event or patch monitoring than a brief 24-hour Holter.

steps: Assess syncope, exertional symptoms, family history and medications.
Obtain ECG and arrange an appropriate duration of ambulatory monitoring.
Treat documented rhythm and contributing triggers based on findings.
Review results and provide urgent return advice for syncope, chest pain or severe breathlessness.
management.safety: Do not label intermittent arrhythmia as anxiety solely because symptoms began during a stressful period.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Asymptomatic inpatient BP elevation / confirm persistent hypertension
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 39-year-old previously normotensive man is observed overnight for ureteric colic. His pain is now well controlled and kidney function is normal, but blood pressure is 165/101 mmHg on two correctly taken ward readings. He has no headache, focal deficit, chest discomfort, pulmonary oedema or ECG abnormalities. He has taken ibuprofen for several days and has no primary care follow-up arranged.
ask: What is the most appropriate plan for his blood pressure?
options: Give an urgent IV antihypertensive infusion until systolic pressure falls below 120 mmHg.
Apply a glyceryl trinitrate patch to prevent silent end-organ damage overnight.
Commence two long-term antihypertensive medications before confirming out-of-hospital readings.
Arrange timely GP review with repeated or ambulatory BP measurements and risk assessment.
Order urgent adrenal CT imaging because a single inpatient BP elevation proves secondary hypertension.
explanations: There is no evidence of hypertensive emergency requiring rapid IV reduction. Overtreatment may cause organ hypoperfusion.
GTN is not indicated for uncomplicated asymptomatic elevated blood pressure and can cause adverse hypotension or headache.

Sustained hypertension should be established with suitable repeat/out-of-office assessment and clinical context before committing to long-term therapy, unless severity/indications demand earlier action.
Correct. Confirm persistence with appropriate home or ambulatory BP measurements, review NSAIDs and cardiovascular risk and ensure follow-up rather than treating one episode aggressively.
Secondary investigations are directed by confirmed hypertension and clues such as hypokalaemia, severe resistance or other suggestive findings, not automatically by isolated ward pressure.
pearl: Raised ward blood pressure without acute organ injury is not synonymous with hypertensive emergency.
pivot: New chest pain, stroke signs, acute pulmonary oedema or other organ injury changes the pathway to urgent hypertensive-emergency assessment.

steps: Repeat BP after rest with an appropriate cuff and check symptoms.
Review medications, renal function, ECG and acute triggers.
Avoid reflex rapid BP lowering without end-organ injury.
Organise timely primary-care BP confirmation and cardiovascular prevention.
management.safety: Do not cause precipitous hypotension by treating an isolated asymptomatic ward reading too aggressively.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Anastomotic leak / fever tachycardia and postoperative ileus
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 58-year-old underwent a colorectal resection with primary anastomosis four days ago. He remains distended, has not passed flatus and complains of worsening abdominal discomfort. His pulse is 124/min, temperature 38.6°C and BP 98/64 mmHg. The abdomen is diffusely tender; the surgical wound is clean and there is no respiratory source of infection. The ward team suggests simple postoperative constipation.
ask: Which complication must be excluded most urgently?
options: Uncomplicated postoperative constipation without systemic infection or anastomotic complication.
Transient postoperative ileus that is expected to improve without further surgical assessment.
A purely medication-related motility disturbance from intermittent opioid analgesia alone.
Functional abdominal bloating related to recent low oral intake and reduced mobility.
Colorectal anastomotic leak causing intra-abdominal sepsis and impaired bowel function.
explanations: Constipation can occur after surgery, but cannot safely explain fever, marked tachycardia and worsening diffuse abdominal tenderness.
Ileus can coexist with an anastomotic leak. It should not be assumed benign when fever and haemodynamic compromise develop.
Opioids may slow bowel motility, but the systemic inflammatory and haemodynamic findings require investigation beyond medication-related constipation.
Reduced mobility and oral intake are common, yet are unlikely to cause this combination of systemic toxicity and worsening pain.

Correct. Anastomotic leak can present with persistent ileus, abdominal pain, fever and tachycardia. Escalate immediately for sepsis resuscitation and senior surgical evaluation, with CT and source control as indicated.
pearl: New tachycardia, fever and prolonged ileus after bowel anastomosis are red flags for anastomotic leakage.
pivot: A well patient with gradually improving symptoms and no systemic signs may have uncomplicated postoperative ileus, but this requires reassessment.

steps: Recognise postoperative sepsis physiology and alert surgery.
Obtain blood tests, cultures and contrast imaging when clinically appropriate.
Give resuscitation and antibiotics while planning drainage or operative source control.
Monitor perfusion and organ function under a senior surgical plan.
management.safety: A clean external incision cannot exclude a dangerous intra-abdominal anastomotic complication.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Digoxin accumulation with AKI / narrow therapeutic index
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 77-year-old taking digoxin for atrial fibrillation presents with nausea, vivid yellow-green visual halos and weakness after several days of poor oral intake. He has also taken ibuprofen for arthritis. His pulse is 43/min, creatinine has risen significantly from baseline and potassium is mildly high. Serum digoxin concentration is above the laboratory reference interval.
ask: Which pharmacological principle best explains why a modest change in elimination causes toxicity?
options: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index and reduced renal clearance can cause accumulation.
Digoxin has an extremely wide therapeutic index that usually protects against toxicity.
Ibuprofen irreversibly activates digoxin receptors and causes a permanent pharmacodynamic effect.
Digoxin undergoes complete presystemic hepatic metabolism independent of renal function.
The primary phenomenon is tachyphylaxis, meaning progressively reduced effect during regular dosing.
explanations: Correct. A small margin between therapeutic and toxic exposure, together with kidney dysfunction, increases risk of dysrhythmia and neurological or gastrointestinal toxicity. Stop exposure and assess severity promptly.
Digoxin has a comparatively narrow safety margin; a modest increase in blood concentration can be clinically important.
NSAIDs can contribute to acute renal impairment and digoxin accumulation, but are not known to work by irreversible direct activation of digoxin receptors.
Renal elimination is clinically important, particularly in older patients and when renal function declines.
Tachyphylaxis describes diminishing response with repeated drug exposure, not heightened toxic effects from accumulation.
pearl: Digoxin toxicity may cause nausea, visual disturbance and bradyarrhythmias, especially with acute kidney injury.
pivot: Life-threatening dysrhythmia, shock or other severe toxicity may require urgent digoxin immune Fab rather than observation alone.

steps: Assess ABCDE, continuous ECG, renal function, electrolytes and digoxin exposure.
Withhold digoxin and review interacting medicines and potassium.
Seek toxicology advice; provide antidote/supportive care according to clinical severity.
Reassess kidney recovery and long-term rate or rhythm management.
management.safety: Serum digoxin level must be interpreted with timing and clinical findings; serious toxicity can occur without an extreme number.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Ovarian torsion / normal Doppler does not exclude
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 23-year-old presents with sudden severe left iliac fossa pain and repeated vomiting. Pregnancy test is negative, and a prior scan showed a 7-cm simple left ovarian cyst. Current pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged ovary with a small amount of free pelvic fluid; Doppler demonstrates some arterial and venous flow. Pain continues despite analgesia, and examination shows marked unilateral tenderness.
ask: Which management is most appropriate despite the Doppler finding?
options: Discharge with simple analgesia because arterial Doppler signals rule out ovarian torsion.
Request immediate gynaecology assessment for possible operative evaluation of torsion.
Give empirical antibiotics for pelvic inflammatory disease before any specialist discussion.
Repeat Doppler imaging in a week once the ovarian swelling has had time to resolve.
Arrange an outpatient MRI as the definitive test before deciding whether torsion is possible.
explanations: Preserved blood flow does not exclude torsion, particularly with intermittent twisting or dual ovarian blood supply. Discharge risks ovarian ischaemia.

Correct. Sudden unilateral pain, vomiting and an enlarged cystic ovary carry significant suspicion. Early gynaecological assessment and possible laparoscopy take precedence over reassurance from partial Doppler flow.
PID is a differential in pelvic pain, but sudden severe onset and vomiting with an adnexal mass is more concerning for torsion. Antibiotics do not reverse twisting.
A week of delay can result in ovarian necrosis and loss of fertility. A normal or equivocal Doppler trace is not a safe reason for observation in this high-probability case.
MRI may help in uncertain non-emergency pelvic pathology but should not delay specialist surgical decision-making for suspected acute torsion.
pearl: Ovarian torsion is a clinical-surgical diagnosis; Doppler blood flow does not reliably exclude it.
pivot: An ectopic pregnancy remains important with a positive pregnancy test, regardless of known ovarian cysts.

steps: Assess haemodynamics, pain and pregnancy status urgently.
Review targeted pelvic ultrasound while keeping torsion on the differential.
Call gynaecology promptly and prepare for surgery if indicated.
Provide postoperative and fertility follow-up based on findings.
management.safety: Do not equate detectable arterial flow with a viable untwisted ovary.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Postoperative drain / biochemical identification of leak
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 61-year-old has an abdominal drain left after complicated pelvic surgery. On day three, its output abruptly increases to 600 mL of straw-coloured fluid in 24 hours. The creatinine concentration in the drain fluid is 570 µmol/L, while her simultaneous serum creatinine is 72 µmol/L. She is mildly tachycardic but afebrile and has no jaundice.
ask: Which explanation most directly fits the laboratory relationship?
options: A bile leak demonstrated by a disproportionately raised fluid bilirubin concentration.
A pancreatic fistula indicated by markedly increased fluid amylase concentration.
A urinary tract leak reflected by drain creatinine much higher than serum creatinine.
A chylous leak demonstrated by elevated triglycerides and typically milky drainage.
An uncomplicated inflammatory serous collection with drain chemistry equal to blood plasma.
explanations: Bile leak would be supported by fluid bilirubin elevation compared with serum, not a distinctive high drain creatinine-to-serum ratio.
Pancreatic leakage is assessed using drain amylase and surgical context; creatinine excess does not specifically suggest it.
Correct. Drain fluid creatinine far exceeding the paired serum level suggests urine, prompting urgent assessment of possible urinary tract injury or leak and urology/surgical consultation.
Chylous drainage is usually characterised by triglyceride-rich fluid after lymphatic injury, not marked creatinine elevation.
Ordinary serous fluid generally does not have a creatinine concentration many times higher than serum; that disparity suggests an additional source.
pearl: Fluid bilirubin suggests bile, amylase pancreatic, triglycerides chyle and creatinine urine.
pivot: A clear or straw-coloured drain does not rule out urinary leakage; compare drain and serum concentrations.

steps: Review procedure, abdominal and urinary symptoms, fluid balance and vitals.
Compare drain creatinine with serum and request targeted imaging as advised.
Contact the operating surgeon and relevant urology specialists promptly.
Manage catheter drainage, repair or diversion as clinically indicated.
management.safety: Do not dismiss a rising postoperative drain volume without examining its biochemical composition and source.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Tetanus-prone puncture / booster after complete primary series
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A healthy 33-year-old gardener steps on a nail embedded in soil. The puncture goes through her shoe into the sole of her foot. She completed her primary tetanus vaccinations and received her most recent booster eight years ago. The wound is irrigated and examined; there is no evidence of immunodeficiency or gross devitalised tissue.
ask: Which tetanus prophylaxis is most appropriate?
options: Provide neither a vaccine nor immunoglobulin because primary immunisation was completed.
Administer tetanus immunoglobulin alone because every puncture requires passive protection.
Provide tetanus toxoid vaccine and immunoglobulin regardless of previous vaccination history.
Give an indicated tetanus-containing booster without routine tetanus immunoglobulin.
Give two separate booster doses immediately rather than following standard wound prevention.
explanations: The wound is tetanus-prone and the last booster was more than five years ago, so a booster is generally indicated.
A fully vaccinated immunocompetent adult does not routinely need immunoglobulin for this presentation; passive protection is primarily for incomplete or uncertain protection in tetanus-prone wounds.
Giving both is unnecessary for someone with a completed primary course and an appropriate vaccination history, unless special indications exist.

Correct. A contaminated deep puncture warrants a booster when the last tetanus dose was five or more years earlier. TIG is not routinely indicated after a full primary series in an immunocompetent person.
Two boosters at once do not improve immediate prevention and increase unnecessary vaccine exposure; follow the recommended interval and documentation.
pearl: A dirty puncture wound generally needs a booster after five years, compared with longer intervals for clean minor wounds.
pivot: Incomplete primary vaccination, unknown history or significant immunodeficiency changes immunoglobulin assessment.

steps: Irrigate, assess depth and remove contamination safely.
Confirm immunisation history and wound classification.
Provide infection, retained-foreign-body and wound-review advice.
management.safety: Tetanus management complements wound cleaning; do not automatically prescribe TIG to fully vaccinated adults.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Acute otitis externa / canal localisation and non-ototoxic drops
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 17-year-old swimmer has increasing left ear pain for four days with watery discharge and pain on chewing. Pulling the pinna or pressing the tragus is very painful. Otoscopy reveals an inflamed oedematous external canal with debris; the drum cannot be clearly visualised. She has no mastoid tenderness, fever or recent upper respiratory symptoms.
ask: Which initial management approach best fits the likely condition?
options: Prescribe oral amoxicillin for presumed acute bacterial otitis media with perforation.
Arrange immediate mastoid surgery because tragal tenderness indicates deep mastoid infection.
Treat with oral antihistamines alone because blocked Eustachian tube is the likely mechanism.
Instil alcohol-based drying drops despite uncertainty about tympanic membrane integrity.
Treat acute otitis externa with appropriate non-ototoxic topical drops and canal care.
explanations: Otitis media can produce discharge after perforation, but tragal/pinna manipulation pain and swollen canal localise the infection externally. Routine oral amoxicillin is not first line.
Mastoiditis is associated with systemic illness, postauricular signs or mastoid tenderness, none described. It still merits reassessment if red flags develop.
Eustachian tube dysfunction causes pressure and conductive hearing change but would not usually produce marked tragal tenderness and canal swelling.
Alcohol or potentially ototoxic drops should be avoided when the tympanic membrane may be perforated; their use could worsen pain or cause injury.
Correct. Acute otitis externa is likely. Use analgesia, topical quinolone or other non-ototoxic therapy safe if drum status is uncertain, and consider a wick for severe canal oedema.
pearl: Tragal and pinna tenderness with canal swelling strongly suggest otitis externa rather than middle-ear infection.
pivot: Diabetes, immunocompromise, cranial nerve symptoms or severe unremitting pain warrant assessment for necrotising otitis externa.

steps: Assess pain, ear canal, pinna, mastoid and red flags.
Avoid forceful irrigation when tympanic membrane status is uncertain.
Treat with adequate analgesia and safe topical therapy; consider a wick.
Keep ear dry and review if worsening or not improving.
management.safety: Use non-ototoxic drops if perforation cannot be excluded and refer severe or complicated infection.
management.local: Apply current Australian guidelines and local health-service pathways.

skill: Quinsy / asymmetric peritonsillar swelling and airway risk
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 25-year-old develops worsening unilateral throat pain and difficulty swallowing after four days of fever. His voice sounds muffled and he can only open his mouth a small amount. On examination, the left peritonsillar area is swollen and pushes the uvula to the right; he has tender ipsilateral cervical nodes. He is breathing comfortably but struggles to swallow water.
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate pathway?
options: Peritonsillar abscess needing prompt ENT assessment, hydration, antibiotics and drainage evaluation.
Uncomplicated viral pharyngitis managed with oral fluids and no further same-day clinical review.
Isolated epiglottitis confirmed by the lateralised peritonsillar swelling and displaced uvula.
Primary dental abscess with no need to examine the upper airway or swallowing function.
Bilateral acute tonsillitis requiring reassurance because uvular displacement is a routine feature.
explanations: Correct. Quinsy commonly causes unilateral peritonsillar fullness, uvular displacement, trismus, muffled voice and severe odynophagia; assess airway and hydration, treat infection and consider drainage.
Simple viral pharyngitis does not usually produce significant trismus or one-sided bulging that displaces the uvula. Reassurance alone risks progression.
Epiglottitis can produce severe sore throat and drooling, but the described localised peritonsillar asymmetry with uvular deviation points elsewhere.
Dental infection can spread to deep neck spaces but would require corresponding oral or floor-of-mouth findings; do not ignore the apparent peritonsillar collection.
Tonsillitis can produce exudative swollen tonsils, yet marked unilateral peritonsillar bulge and uvular deviation are characteristic complications, not ordinary symmetry.
pearl: Trismus, muffled voice and displaced uvula are classic clues to a peritonsillar abscess.
pivot: Drooling, stridor or worsening work of breathing require urgent airway team support before an invasive throat examination.

steps: Assess airway, ability to swallow, hydration and sepsis signs.
Examine carefully and obtain ENT review; imaging only if needed for deep-neck spread.
Give analgesia, hydration and appropriate antibiotics with drainage planning.
Observe response and provide return instructions if managed without admission.
management.safety: Never attempt blind bedside drainage when airway compromise or unexpected deep-neck anatomy is suspected.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local senior-led management.

skill: New central facial palsy / stroke pathway despite anticoagulation
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 76-year-old woman taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation notices sudden left lower facial drooping and slurred speech on waking. She is able to raise both eyebrows symmetrically and close both eyes tightly, but the left corner of her mouth does not move normally. She has no ear pain, rash or recent facial injury; the last-known-well time is uncertain.
ask: What action best addresses the likely process?
options: Treat presumed Bell palsy with oral prednisolone and review in the community next week.
Activate urgent stroke assessment for possible right cerebral hemispheric ischaemia.
Discontinue anticoagulation and arrange routine cranial nerve physiotherapy alone.
Prescribe oral antibiotics for facial cellulitis without performing neurovascular examination.
Book outpatient dental evaluation because facial asymmetry can follow dental infection.
explanations: A peripheral Bell palsy usually involves forehead, eye closure and mouth on the same side. Forehead sparing plus sudden dysarthria is concerning for a central lesion.

Correct. Abrupt contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing suggests an upper motor neuron lesion; anticoagulation reduces but does not eliminate stroke risk. Urgent imaging and stroke-team assessment are required.

Unsupervised cessation of anticoagulation may increase stroke risk and does not diagnose the new focal deficit. Acute treatment decisions depend on neuroimaging, timing and the responsible stroke team.
Facial cellulitis causes local redness, swelling or tenderness rather than isolated sudden lower facial motor weakness with dysarthria.
Dental infection may cause pain and swelling, but should not distract from acute focal neurological deficits and vascular risk factors.
pearl: Forehead sparing suggests a central facial weakness pattern; stroke remains possible despite a DOAC.
pivot: A complete ipsilateral upper- and lower-face weakness without additional central features may suggest peripheral CN VII palsy, but needs clinical assessment.

steps: Document last-known-well and perform a focused stroke screen and glucose check.
Activate stroke team and urgent brain/vascular imaging as indicated.
Manage airway, BP, anticoagulation implications and reperfusion decisions with specialists.
Arrange swallow screening, rehabilitation and secondary prevention.
management.safety: Do not administer thrombolysis without specialised assessment of anticoagulant timing and eligibility.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local senior-led management.

skill: Isolated vomiting / reconsider gastroenteritis
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 21-month-old child has vomited repeatedly for six hours and has refused his usual feeds. He has not passed stool today and there has been no diarrhoea. There is no known household illness. He looks tired but is rousable, has a slightly prolonged capillary refill and a soft abdomen between brief episodes of crying. The initial triage label is 'viral gastroenteritis'.
ask: Which feature should particularly prompt reconsideration of that working diagnosis?
options: The lack of a recognised contact with another vomiting person.
The mild tachycardia that can accompany reduced oral intake.
The absence of diarrhoea alongside frequent vomiting in a toddler.
The presence of nausea after attempted feeding following several vomits.
The parent reporting that he seems quieter than during his last cold.
explanations: Many gastrointestinal infections have no identified contact, so exposure history alone is a weak discriminator.
Mild tachycardia may reflect distress or dehydration and does not uniquely indicate a surgical problem.

Correct. Isolated vomiting without diarrhoea warrants assessment for other causes including intussusception, obstruction, urinary infection or intracranial pathology, especially with episodic pain or altered behaviour.
Feeding can trigger nausea in common viral illness as well as obstruction; this finding alone is not especially distinctive.
Reduced activity is concerning if substantial, but is nonspecific without its pattern and severity. The missing diarrhoea warns against prematurely assuming gastroenteritis.
pearl: Vomiting is not synonymous with gastroenteritis; bilious emesis, episodic pain or drowsiness are important alternate-diagnosis clues.
pivot: If green bilious vomiting develops, urgently assess for bowel obstruction and surgical emergencies.

steps: Assess hydration, perfusion, activity and glucose.
Check abdominal examination, urine and focused imaging if intussusception/obstruction suspected.
Treat dehydration and address the established cause.
Safety-net for bilious emesis, worsening pain, lethargy or reduced urine output.
management.safety: Do not ignore intermittent severe pain or altered consciousness merely because the abdomen is soft between episodes.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local senior-led management.

skill: Ottawa ankle rules / no x-ray for isolated ligament tenderness
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 27-year-old netball player twists her left ankle while landing. She walks four steps in the clinic, and tenderness is located just anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus along the ligament. There is no tenderness over the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, the navicular or the base of the fifth metatarsal. Neurovascular examination is normal.
ask: Which imaging strategy is most appropriate for this presentation?
options: Obtain an ankle radiograph because ligament-region pain meets the malleolar bone tenderness criterion.
Obtain both ankle and foot radiographs because any twisting injury risks an occult midfoot fracture.
Order an ankle ultrasound as a mandatory test before diagnosing an uncomplicated ligament sprain.
Use Ottawa criteria to avoid routine radiography and provide a supportive ankle injury plan.
Obtain ankle CT before functional rehabilitation despite negative clinical radiograph criteria.
explanations: Ottawa malleolar criteria refer to bony tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of the malleoli or inability to bear weight, not merely anterior ligament tenderness.
The absence of base-of-fifth and navicular bony pain plus weight-bearing ability makes routine midfoot imaging unnecessary by the specified rules.
Ultrasound is not mandatory in a straightforward low-risk ankle sprain and usually does not change early conservative treatment.
Correct. Ability to walk four steps and lack of designated malleolar or midfoot bone tenderness support no immediate radiograph, while providing early mobilisation advice and safety-netting.
CT is generally reserved for selected suspected complex fractures or cases where initial assessment indicates it; it is not a standard first step here.
pearl: Ottawa ankle rules use specific bony landmarks and the ability to take four steps, not simply pain after inversion.
pivot: Rules are less reliable in certain contexts, including some neuropathic or unreliable examination settings; reassess clinical judgement.

steps: Inspect swelling, deformity, tenderness points and neurovascular status.
Apply Ottawa ankle and foot criteria carefully.
Provide analgesia, support, ice as appropriate and graded weight bearing.
Review persistent pain, instability or inability to mobilise as expected.
management.safety: Do not document 'no bony tenderness' without checking the posterior malleolar margins and foot landmarks.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local senior-led management.

skill: Cat bite to hand / prophylaxis for deep puncture
context: Revision Blossom Garden · original case inspired by 2024–2025 Monash paper themes
stem: A 43-year-old attempts to pick up a frightened cat and sustains two small punctures over the dorsal hand near the index metacarpophalangeal joint. The wound looks clean after washing, and she has normal movement without fever or spreading erythema. Her tetanus history is recorded as up to date. She has no penicillin allergy.
ask: Which approach is most appropriate to reduce infection risk?
options: Avoid antibiotics because puncture wounds under 5 mm almost never cause deep infection.
Offer a topical antiseptic alone and close each puncture tightly using tissue adhesive.
Give prophylactic oral flucloxacillin as sole cover without regard to animal oral flora.
Delay prophylaxis until wound culture is positive or local cellulitis has developed.
Thoroughly irrigate and assess the hand, with prophylactic amoxicillin-clavulanate as indicated.
explanations: Cat teeth create narrow punctures that can inoculate bacteria into hand compartments even when the surface looks benign; small size is not reassuring.
Topical cleansing matters but does not reliably prevent deep hand infection, and sealing punctures can trap contamination.
Flucloxacillin alone may not adequately cover key cat oral organisms including Pasteurella; choose prophylaxis based on animal-bite guidance.
Cultures are generally not needed for uninfected initial bites, and waiting for established deep infection can risk joint or tendon complications.
Correct. Examine tendons/joints, irrigate well, avoid routine primary closure of punctures and give recommended prophylactic antibiotics for a high-risk hand bite.
pearl: Cat bites to the hand have high infection risk despite small puncture marks; Pasteurella cover matters.
pivot: Any reduced finger motion, increasing swelling or pain with passive movement warrants urgent hand surgery assessment.

steps: Check hand tendon, joint and neurovascular involvement.
Irrigate thoroughly; assess for retained teeth and tetanus status.
Provide appropriate oral prophylaxis with allergy considerations.
